title: Maximum Path Quality of a Graph
statement:
An undirected graph has `n = values.length` nodes labelled `0` to `n - 1`; node `i` is worth `values[i]`. Each entry `edges[j] = [u, v, time]` joins nodes `u` and `v`, and crossing that edge in either direction takes `time` seconds.

Consider walks that leave node `0`, finish back at node `0`, and spend no more than `maxTime` seconds in total. A walk may pass through nodes and edges repeatedly. Its quality is the sum of `values` over the **distinct** nodes it touches (a node counts once no matter how often it is visited, and node `0` always counts). Return the highest quality any such walk achieves; the walk that never leaves node `0` is allowed.

Every node has at most four edges, no pair of nodes is joined twice, and the graph need not be connected.
constraints: Each node has at most four edges
signature: int maximalPathQuality(int[] values, int[][] edges, int maxTime)
notes:
## Intuition

The limits make exhaustive search affordable. Every edge takes at least 10 seconds and `maxTime` is at most 100, so a walk uses at most 10 edges; with at most four edges per node that is at most about 4^10 ≈ 10^6 walks. So we can try every walk from node `0` by backtracking and record the quality each time the walk is back at `0`.

The only subtlety is scoring repeated visits. Keeping a visit counter per node lets us add a node's value only on its first visit and undo that exactly when we backtrack.

## Approach

1. Build an adjacency list `graph` of `[next, time]` pairs for both directions of every edge.
2. Set `visits[0] = 1` and start `dfs(0, 0, values[0])`.
3. In `dfs(node, elapsed, quality)`, whenever `node` is `0` the walk is a valid closed walk, so update `best`.
4. For each neighbour `next` reachable within `maxTime`, compute `gain` (its value if `visits[next]` is 0, otherwise 0), increment `visits[next]`, recurse, then decrement it to backtrack.
5. Return `best`.

## Example 1, step by step

`values = [0, 32, 10, 43]`, `maxTime = 49`. Going `0 → 1` gives quality 32 at time 10; returning to `0` at time 20 records `best = 32`. From there `0 → 3` adds 43 (time 30, quality 75) and `3 → 0` at time 40 records `best = 75`. Node 2 can never count: reaching it and returning costs `10 + 15 + 15 + 10 = 50 > 49`. The answer is `75`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(4^(maxTime / 10)) in the worst case, about 10^6 calls, plus O(n + edges) to build the graph.
- Space: O(n + edges) for the graph and counters, and recursion depth at most `maxTime / 10`.

## Pitfalls

- Use a visit **count**, not a boolean: after backtracking out of a second visit, the node must still count as visited by the outer path.
- Record `best` only at node `0`, since the walk has to end there.
- Node `0`'s own value always counts, even if no edge can be used.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `graph` | adjacency list of `[next, time]` pairs |
| `visits` | how many times each node is on the current walk |
| `best` | highest quality of a closed walk found so far |
| `node`, `elapsed`, `quality` | current position, time used, and value collected |
| `next`, `time`, `gain` | neighbour, travel time, and value it would add |
